title: Multiple timeframes: one market, several summaries
subtitle: Give each chart a job and respect when its information exists.
takeaway: Different timeframes aggregate the same underlying activity. Use them for distinct questions and keep incomplete bars visibly provisional.

sections.title: Different views need not disagree
paragraphs: A stock can rise across several months, pull back for three days, and rebound over the last hour. A monthly observer, daily observer, and intraday observer may all describe different directions correctly. Trouble begins when one sentence calls the stock bullish without stating the horizon or when the analyst selects whichever chart supports a preferred position. Multiple-timeframe work should make the intended duration clearer rather than provide more opportunities to rationalize a trade.

Think of the higher timeframe as a broad summary and the lower timeframe as greater detail within that summary. Their relationship is aggregation, not a hierarchy of truth. A daily candle can hide several sharp intraday reversals. An intraday reversal may barely affect the weekly close. Decide which behavior matters to your question before moving between charts. A tool chosen for minute-scale decisions should not quietly become the justification for a month-scale holding period.

sections.title: Aggregate consistently, then accept lost information
paragraphs: A weekly OHLC bar uses the first eligible open, highest eligible high, lowest eligible low, and last eligible close within its defined week. Its volume sums eligible interval volume. This construction requires matching session boundaries and adjustment rules. Aggregation discards the order of intermediate observations. Identical weekly candles can arise from very different daily sequences, so the larger bar cannot recover the path that it omitted.

The main 15 daily closes are $100, $102, $101, $104, $105; $106, $107, $105, $104, $103; $104, $106, $108, $107, $110. Group these into three explicitly defined five-session weeks. Their closes are $105, $103, and $110. The prior two completed weekly closes, before the display, are $98 and $99. Daily closes alone do not reveal weekly high or low; intraday extremes are absent.

tables.title: What exists after each daily close

sections.title: Give the weekly and daily views separate jobs
paragraphs: For this demonstration, weekly context is up if the latest completed weekly close exceeds the preceding completed weekly close, otherwise down-or-equal. This is a close-direction teaching classification, not a full higher-high/higher-low trend definition. Daily change describes today’s close compared with yesterday. We then label an upward daily change aligned when completed-week context is up and conflicting when it is down-or-equal. The label compares directions over different intervals; it does not mean either description is wrong, and the developing week is never used to assign it. No order rule is implied.

Before session 5, the known weekly pair is $98→$99, so context is up. After 5, it is $99→$105, still up. During sessions 8 and 9 the daily price falls from $107 to $105 to $104, while last completed weekly close remains $105. This is a daily retreat inside the still-up completed weekly context. The directions differ, but the descriptions do not contradict each other: they cover different intervals. Because the labels apply only to upward daily changes, sessions 8 and 9 receive neither label.

At session 10 the week actually finishes at $103, below prior $105. Context changes to down at that close. Session 11 rises $103→$104, an upward daily change against down completed-week context. The analyst should record a conflict rather than quietly treating the current developing week as already complete. At session 15, the $110 completion changes weekly context back to up.

sections.title: An unfinished higher-timeframe bar is provisional
paragraphs: On Wednesday, this week’s closing price has not yet been established. A weekly RSI, average, or crossover based on the developing close can change by Friday. TradingView’s documentation explains why higher-timeframe requests can repaint as unconfirmed values evolve and why confirmation changes availability. The ordinary updating of a live bar is not inherently improper; presenting its final historical value as known earlier is the problem.

In this same second week, Tuesday session 7 closes $107; Wednesday session 8 closes $105; Friday session 10 closes $103. At Wednesday’s close the current developing weekly close is $105, but the eventual $103 finish is unknown. The last completed weekly close is also $105, from the preceding week, but it is a different observation with a different timestamp. Matching numerical values do not make a developing and completed bar equivalent.

sections.title: Follow the clock rather than interpolate
paragraphs: The confirmed series is $99 after sessions 1–4, $105 after 5–9, $103 after 10–14, and $110 after 15. It holds each established value constant and jumps only at the completion timestamp. The illustration uses a step line: a slope between sessions 4 and 5 would falsely suggest gradual availability of the next final value. Observations are sampled after the daily close; just before the session-5 close, $99 is still the latest confirmed value.

A developing weekly close can be shown separately if it is labeled provisional. In this simplified close-only example, that developing value equals each latest daily close during the week. It changes with the daily line, not the confirmed step series. A reader examining session 9 must not replace it with the session-10 final close.

To check a multi-timeframe note, ask for three fields: decision timestamp, most recent completed higher-timeframe observation, and current lower-timeframe observation. At session 11 they are “after close 11,” “completed week 2 close $103 versus prior $105,” and “daily close $104 versus $103.” That record preserves the labelled conflict without requiring a trade to resolve it.

sections.title: Work through an aligned and a conflicting case
paragraphs: After session 6 closes, daily price rises $105→$106 and completed weekly pair $99→$105 is up: the observations align under the stated close-direction classifications. After session 11 closes, daily price rises $103→$104 while completed weekly pair $105→$103 is down: they conflict. Both statements can be reconstructed from the table without selecting a new interval after the fact.

Suppose a predeclared research filter requires up completed-week context before examining an upward daily change. Session 6 would be eligible and session 11 would not. That is the consequence of this particular filter, not proof that the filtered observation is better. If instead the project studies countertrend daily recoveries, session 11 is relevant precisely because of the conflict. The research question decides the role.

The next chapters add event and execution context; the testing chapter shows how timestamp mistakes contaminate results. For now, the essential achievement is a coherent observation record. Larger intervals summarize overlapping underlying activity, so agreement is informative about scale but not several independent votes. Keep a small set of views tied to the intended question and use the table to settle what was actually known.

example.title: A conflict that the timestamps explain
example.text: At close 11, daily price is $104, above session 10’s $103. The most recent completed weekly pair is $105→$103, so weekly close-direction context is down. A weekly-up eligibility filter excludes this daily rise; a countertrend study could include it. The developing third week has not yet supplied its final $110 close, which arrives only after session 15.

exercise: From the synchronized table, give the latest completed weekly close after sessions 4, 5, 9, 10, 14, and 15. Classify the session-11 daily/weekly relationship.

quiz.question: After session 9 closes, what is the latest completed weekly close?
quiz.explanation: $105 is the completed preceding week; it remains held through session 9.
feedback: $105 is the completed preceding week; it remains held through session 9.
$104 is the current daily close, also the developing week’s current close.
$103 is the future session-10 weekly finish.

figure.title: Daily closes and the last completed weekly close (step series)
figure.caption: The 15 fictional sessions form three five-session weeks. Values are sampled after each daily close. Confirmed weekly close changes only at sessions 5, 10 and 15, to $105, $103 and $110; prior completed closes are $98 and $99. In this close-only example the developing weekly close is the daily line itself. Daily closes do not supply weekly highs/lows.

outcomes: Aggregate daily closes into weekly closes under disclosed boundaries.
Track the last completed weekly value as a step series.
Resolve an apparent daily/weekly conflict using a stated analytical role.

figures.title: What changes at each weekly completion
figures.caption: Each state is sampled after the named daily close, the convention used throughout the chapter.

steps.title: After session 5
steps.text: Known completed pair 99→105: up. Later daily retreat can coexist.

steps.title: After session 10
steps.text: Known completed pair 105→103: down. Session 11 daily rise conflicts.

steps.title: After session 15
steps.text: Known completed pair 103→110: up. New weekly state begins here.

solution: After 4: $99; 5: $105; 9: $105; 10: $103; 14: $103; 15: $110. The step changes only at the three completion points.
At 11 the daily close rises 103→104, while completed weekly close fell 105→103. Under the stated close-direction definition they conflict. The developing week’s eventual $110 cannot be used at 11.

practice.title: Fill the session-8 record
practice.question: After session 8 closes, identify current daily close, prior daily close, latest completed weekly pair, and whether the daily retreat contradicts that weekly state.
solution: Current daily close $105 follows $107, so daily change is −$2. Completed weekly pair remains $99→$105, so weekly context is up.
They describe a daily retreat within completed up-week context. The developing week’s current close $105 is numerically equal to prior completed close, but belongs to a different interval.

practice.title: Spot future information
practice.question: A fresh fictional series defines five-session weeks. Prior completed weekly closes are $48 and $50. Sessions 1–5 close $51, $49, $52, $53, $54; sessions 6–10 close $55, $56, $53, $52, $51. At session 8 close, give the current daily change, latest completed weekly pair and developing weekly close. When does the second displayed week’s $51 close become available, and why are sessions 6–9 not assigned it?
solution: At session 8, the daily move is 53 − 56 = −$3. Completed weekly pair is $50→$54, an up comparison. The developing week currently ends at $53; it is not a completed weekly observation.

The completed $51 weekly close becomes known only after session 10. At sessions 6–9 the latest completed weekly close stays $54. The fresh path contains a daily retreat within completed up-week context; assigning $51 early would borrow future information.

evidence.location: Daily/weekly table, primary chart, worked solutions.
evidence.summary: Derived weekly closes at exactly sessions 5/10/15 and held each last known value until the next completion.
evidence.limits: Five-session weeks simplify calendars and do not assert every real week has five sessions.
